gameplay_summary: Four-player mahjong against computer opponents drawn from Masayuki Katayama's comedy mahjong manga, each playing in their own manga personality.
dossier: Asmik's Famicom mahjong game, developed by Game Arts, based on Masayuki Katayama's Young Magazine manga about a crowd of eccentric, self-centred mahjong players. The series is known for its opponents playing in character: reviewing Game Arts' earlier computer version, Jun Sasaki praised AI routines that clearly reflected each character's personality, along with in-game speech. The manga is also famous for absurd joke variants such as sushi mahjong and job-hunting mahjong, but the sources don't say whether any of these appear here. Later games in the series added characters from Katayama's Super Zugan. The Famicom version's own feature set isn't detailed in the sources.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Mahjong itself is universal for players who know it, but menus, yaku and character dialogue are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Journey to the West reskin of Wonder Boy in Monster Land: as Son Goku, fight through side-scrolling areas, earn money, buy weapons, armour and items in shops, and defeat the Bull Demon King to rescue Sanzo.
dossier: Jaleco's Famicom version of Westone and Sega's 1987 arcade Wonder Boy in Monster Land, with the characters replaced by figures from Journey to the West. Son Goku sets out to rescue the kidnapped monk Sanzo from the Bull Demon King. The core system is Monster Land's: side-scrolling action-RPG stages, money from defeated enemies, and shops and hidden rooms selling better swords, shields, armour and magic. Unlike the original, Goku starts clothed and his look changes with his gear, and there's no visible timer, though time still slowly drains your life. Hakkai and Gojo appear only in hidden events. The title screen shows NMK's logo, but former staff say NMK wasn't involved. A Switch re-release in 2024 added extensive help features.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The action is visual, but shop names, item descriptions and the hints that matter for progress are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. Wonder Boy in Monster Land itself had no NES release.

gameplay_summary: Buzzer quiz for one to four players: answer choices appear one by one after each question, and whoever buzzes in first answers, scoring or losing points, with special double and 'devil' questions.
dossier: Athena's quiz game for up to four players. It's built around fast-buzzer quizzing. After the question appears, the answer choices are revealed gradually, and you hit your button as soon as you think you know, then answer. Right answers, wrong answers and timeouts move your score up or down, and the first to reach the target score, or the leader at the end, wins. Occasional 'Double Quiz' questions are worth twice the points, and 'Devil Quiz' questions let you sabotage a rival. The sources don't say how four players connect.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A Japanese-language quiz; the questions and answers are the whole game.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Fantasy RPG in Sheldorado, a world of shell-backed creatures: as the fire-shell boy Ricky, reunite the scattered heroes Kupikupi, Poyon and Bab and defeat the demon king Fat Badger.
dossier: Namco's RPG, developed by Birthday, and the start of a series continued mostly by Hudson. Its official English subtitle is Shell Saurs Story. In Sheldorado, people live alongside 'kaijuu', creatures that carry shells on their backs. The fire-shell boy Ricky has to gather his companions Kupikupi, Poyon and Bab, who've been flung across the world, and together defeat the demon king Fat Badger. The box was lavish: alongside the cartridge and manual it held figures of the four heroes, a world map, and a sealed envelope called the 'secret letter of tears'. Readers rated it highly (24.66/30 in Famicom Magazine), though levelling was considered a grind. It returned in 2020 as Namcot Collection DLC.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A text-driven RPG with Japanese menus, dialogue and story.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: The original box included four character figures, a world map and a sealed 'secret letter of tears'; complete copies should have these.

gameplay_summary: Half-court street basketball, one-on-one or two-on-two, with an optional winners'-outs rule and an 'around the world' shooting mode.
dossier: Jaleco's 'Moero!!' street basketball game, played on a half court as one-on-one or two-on-two. You can turn winners' outs on or off, and an 'around the world' mode is just about making baskets, without the fouls of the standard game. Like Double Dribble, it uses slow-motion sequences for big plays. Contemporary reviews were positive; later writers called it old-fashioned, with predictable opponents.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Basketball is visual; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Hoops (1989).

gameplay_summary: Hardboiled amnesia mystery: as private eye Ace Harding, wake up in a 1940s Chicago bar with no memory and a corpse upstairs, and use command menus on the scene to clear your name.
dossier: Kemco's command-select version of ICOM's 1985 MacVenture adventure, and a Famitsu Silver Hall of Fame game. In December 1941 Chicago, ex-boxer turned private eye Ace Harding wakes up in a bathroom stall at Joe's Bar with no memory, while a dead man upstairs sets him up for murder. A strap-down chair, mysterious vials and a needle mark hint at what happened. You pick verbs like move, examine and open and point at objects in the picture. The 'self' command, used across the MacVenture games, starts here, and it can be grimly funny: turning the gun on yourself gets a weary line and an immediate game over.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A text adventure; descriptions, clues and dialogue are in Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Déjà Vu (1990), with some content replaced; for example, the game-over skull became a tombstone.
japanese_version_notes: The game-over screen shows a talking skull; the overseas NES version changed it to a tombstone, and the ja.wikipedia master list notes some other content was replaced for North America.

gameplay_summary: Namco's second Family Mahjong game; the sources don't describe what this sequel adds.
dossier: Namco's sequel to Family Mahjong (1987), developed by Nichibutsu. The first game was a two-player mahjong game aimed at beginners, with lessons on tiles, scoring and hands (including a famous arithmetic error in its points tutorial) and quizzes. The ja.wikipedia article covers only that first game, and no source in the snapshot describes this sequel's modes or what the 'Road to Shanghai' subtitle refers to, so its contents are unconfirmed.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Mahjong can be played with knowledge of the rules, but menus and any lesson or story text are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Dice-driven Sengoku board game with Beat Takeshi as advisor and nuisance: race across Japan, seek employment at castles, climb to daimyo by service or betrayal, then conquer the country, plus party games.
dossier: Taito's follow-up of sorts to the notorious Takeshi no Chousenjou. This one is a sane, structured board game, and it's unclear how much Beat Takeshi actually contributed. You roll dice across Sengoku Japan (minus Okinawa) while 'Lord Takeshi' pops up to advise or interfere. The Sengoku Game has linked modes. A race from Abashiri Castle to Takeshi Castle ends in a golf duel needing a hole-in-one. A job hunt as a masterless samurai needs a letter of introduction and then skill, a bribe or a comedy routine to get hired. A career mode is won by loyal service or by overthrowing your lord. A unification mode is won by war or politics. A separate Party Game mode is included.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Events, Takeshi's interjections and the career system are all Japanese text.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Chinese-astrology fortune-telling software; the sources give no detail.
dossier: A Jaleco-published release (product code SAN-CQ), developed by Aicom and released on November 29, 1988. The title means 'Chinese astrology', and the census lists it as fortune-telling software. There's no ja.wikipedia article for it in the research snapshot and FamiWiki has no description, so what readings it offers and how it's used aren't documented in the sources consulted.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Fortune-telling software is presumably all Japanese text; not confirmed.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling action: stranded on a monster island, fight through six zones with a rifle that becomes a club when out of ammo, and take a drug to transform into the hulking Macho Man, whose health depends on your score.
dossier: Vic Tokai's action game, developed by Aicom. In the Japanese story, the scientist Jackson flies to Troppo Island to deliver a new drug, is shot down, and has to fight across the island. The monsters have stolen the drug, Macho Max Pellets, and taking one turns him into the powerful Macho Man. There are six zones of two areas each. Normally you shoot a rifle with limited ammo, which you swing as a club when it runs out, both weak. Bosses are close to unbeatable without transforming, some soaking up nearly 100 shots. As Macho Man you punch hard, fire chest beams at a health cost, and get one hit point per 5,000 points scored beforehand. The final boss looks very like the Flatwoods Monster.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Amagon (1989).
japanese_version_notes: The hero is the scientist Jackson, who becomes Macho Man with the Macho Max drug; the NES version made him the marine Amagon, who becomes Megagon with a Mega-Key.

gameplay_summary: Overhead run-and-gun: as Ricky or Mary, rescue captured comrades aboard alien-infested ships against a time bomb, then defeat each ship's grotesque guardian, alone or with two players at once.
dossier: Sunsoft's Famicom port of Sega's 1987 arcade game, developed by Sanritsu. In space year 2089, aliens have taken colonists prisoner aboard their ships, and soldiers Ricky and Mary go in to free them. In each stage a time bomb is ticking. You rescue enough hostages to open the exit, then destroy the stage boss before time runs out, across seven stages, the last a boss fight. Weapon caches change your shot type. The aliens' grotesque, Alien-inspired designs gave the arcade game its atmosphere. Unlike Sega's own heavily cut-down Mark III version, the Famicom port aims to reproduce the arcade game, keeping scrolling stages and simultaneous two-player play.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Shooting action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Alien Syndrome by Tengen (unlicensed, December 1989): the same Sanritsu port under a different publisher.

gameplay_summary: Railway board game for up to four players: roll to travel Japan by train toward your own destination, earn grants and buy railway lines and local businesses, and finish with the highest total assets.
dossier: Hudson's first Momotaro Dentetsu, a self-parody of its RPG Momotaro Densetsu by the same staff, and the start of one of Japan's best-loved party series. Many series fixtures came later, though. Here each player has a different destination, there are no plus or minus stations, no player-attacking events and no Bonbi poverty god, so competition is mild. You start at Tokyo with a ¥1 million grant and a ¥2 million rail line. Each year has four seasonal turns: roll one die to move, then two dice for an event, with summer bringing income and winter costs. Reaching any property station counts, with bigger grants for longer trips, and you can buy railway sections as well as businesses. Reviewers found it more fun in a group than alone.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The board play is visual, but events, station names and purchases are Japanese text.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Comic real-time strategy: as the inexperienced young lord of Almamoon, rebuild your army and finances, command generals and summon monsters from magic eggs, and reconquer a continent split among rival powers.
dossier: Square's first Hanjuku Hero, directed by Takashi Tokita. King Darkfried of Almamoon unified the continent with mysterious 'eggs' and his knights, then died the next day, and every conquered nation rebelled. His half-baked heir is left with one castle, a few loyal retainers, and no idea how to use the eggs. Behind the comic look it's one of the series' toughest entries: income and expenses are tightly balanced, battles are hard, and there's no single final boss, just up to eleven rival nations to conquer. Its three episodes differ mainly in map and number of enemies, and only clearing the hardest third gives the staff-roll ending. Later entries leaned much further into gags and parody.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Strategy and economy menus, events and the series' humour are all Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Fast ninja action-platformer with cinematic cut-scenes: as Ryu Hayabusa, wall-cling, slash and use ninja arts through American cities and ruins to uncover the truth behind his father's death.
dossier: Tecmo's Ninja Ryukenden, the second 'Tecmo Theater' game and famous for its cinematic cut-scenes. Before a duel he never returns from, Ryu Hayabusa's father leaves him the Dragon Sword and a letter telling him to go to America and find his old friend, archaeologist Walter Smith. In America Ryu is attacked by a mysterious army, saves a woman, and is then knocked out by her tranquilliser dart. She gives him a strange statue and tells him to run. The trail leads to the demon statues Walter and Ryu's father found in Amazon ruins. Its working titles included 'Dragon Ninja' and 'Ninja Gaiden'. The NES version is a translation with some character names changed.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — The action needs no reading; the Japanese cut-scenes carry the story but aren't needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Ninja Gaiden (1989).
japanese_version_notes: The Japanese original's cut-scene names differ from the NES version's (for example, Ryu's father is Jo Hayabusa rather than Ken).

gameplay_summary: Kaiju action-strategy: move Godzilla and Mothra like pieces across hex-grid planet boards, then play each hex as a side-scrolling stage, fighting Planet X's monsters and invasion forces.
dossier: Toho's Godzilla game, developed by Compile. In the year 2XXX, Planet X appears when Pluto and Neptune swap positions, and its people invade Earth with an army of space monsters. Godzilla teams up with Mothra and Earth's forces to repel them. Each planet is a hex board where you move the two monsters like chess pieces, and every hex opens a side-scrolling stage: rocky, jungle, city or hyperspace zones. Hyperspace zones bring fights with Matango, Dogora and the Gotengo. The alien ships echo Atragon and The War in Space. The North American release dropped the Toho Cenfile-Soft Library and Compile credits.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Godzilla: Monster of Monsters! (1989).
japanese_version_notes: Credits Toho Cenfile-Soft Library and Compile; the NES version credits Toho Eizo instead.

gameplay_summary: Simulation-leaning Formula One racing: drive the sixteen-race world championship calendar, braking hard for real corners, shifting gears manually and pitting for worn tyres.
dossier: Varie's first Famicom release, developed by Human, starring Satoru Nakajima, the first Japanese full-time F1 driver. It runs the full sixteen-race F1 calendar and was far more demanding than arcade-style racers. The circuits have accurate sharp and sweeping corners that need real braking, most cars require manual gear changes, sometimes dozens per lap, and tyre wear means at least one pit stop per race. It started Varie's long F-1 Hero series. The North American release replaced Nakajima with CART driver Michael Andretti.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Racing; the menus are simple.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Michael Andretti's World GP (1990).
japanese_version_notes: Endorsed by Satoru Nakajima; the NES version is endorsed by Michael Andretti.

gameplay_summary: Fantasy turn-based wargame: capture cities for funds, hire units like fighters and goblins at your castle, exploit matchups between unit types, and defeat the enemy King, in a campaign or a multiplayer mode with alliances.
dossier: Atlus's fantasy strategy game for Namco, a Famitsu Silver Hall of Fame game. Each side is led by its King, and the enemy King (Lucifer, in the four-scenario campaign 'Battle with Lucifer') has to be defeated. You capture cities for funds and hire units at castles where your King is stationed. Unit types such as fighters and goblins have attack and defence values that change depending on the opponent, so matchups decide battles. The multiplayer mode supports up to four players, with alliances for team play. Kazuma Kaneko worked on the characters, which fed into Megami Tensei. The cartridge uses all eight channels of Namco's 163 sound chip. It was praised as approachable and well balanced.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The map play is visual, but unit names, stats and menus are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: The cartridge uses Namco's 163 expansion sound chip.

gameplay_summary: Nine-star astrology fortune-telling software for 1989; the sources give no further detail.
dossier: Fortune-telling software developed by Micronics and published by Jingukan Polaris, based on Japanese nine-star (kyuusei) astrology with 1989 readings. FamiWiki records the release and a September 1988 Family Computer Magazine print ad, but there's no ja.wikipedia article in the research snapshot, and how the readings work isn't documented in the sources consulted.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Fortune-telling software is text by nature, presumably all Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Toei Animation release developed by Thinking Rabbit; the sources give no gameplay detail.
dossier: A Toei Animation release developed by Thinking Rabbit (8 Eyes, Sokoban). FamiWiki lists it as single-player and links to StrategyWiki and The Cutting Room Floor pages, but it has no description itself, and there's no ja.wikipedia article in the research snapshot. Its genre, which the title suggests is fighting-based, and its gameplay are unconfirmed in the sources consulted.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Unknown; rated provisionally until the game's text dependence is confirmed.

gameplay_summary: Famicom port of the computer game Shin Taketori Monogatari, based on the Princess Kaguya folk tale; the sources give no gameplay detail.
dossier: Victor's Famicom release, developed by Micronics. According to the ja.wikipedia master list, it's a port of 'Shin Taketori Monogatari', released for the PC-8801 and other computers and based on the Japanese folk tale of the bamboo cutter and Princess Kaguya. No article for the game was captured, and FamiWiki has no description, so its genre (probably an adventure, given its computer origin) and gameplay are unconfirmed.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A computer-adventure port would be text-driven in Japanese; not confirmed.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Treasure Island-inspired sword platformer: as young sailor Jim, slash through six stages of pirates and animals to Captain Silver's treasure, buying gear with collected money and gathering letters for extra lives.
dossier: Tokuma Shoten's Famicom version of Data East's 1987 arcade game, loosely based on Treasure Island. Young Jim hears of Captain Silver's treasure from an old man aboard ship and sets off past pirates, natives and animals to find it. He fights with a sword, and catching fairies lets it fire shots that power up in stages. Money from enemies buys items in shops, though stage 2 has none, and collecting the letters of 'CAPTAIN SILVER' earns a life. The Famicom version reworks the arcade. There are six stages, bonus rounds after all but stage 5, and a life meter where a hit costs two points. Each stage has a helpful old woman who advises and heals, and a nuisance hag who misleads you or halves your life. The attack voices are gone.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The action is visual, but the old women's advice and the shops are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Roster update of Ultimate Harikiri Stadium: the same baseball game with player growth, joke teams and series quirks, with player data refreshed for 1988.
dossier: Taito's minor revision of its first 'Hari-Sta' baseball game, released about six months later, which updates only the player data. Everything else is the original. Batting uses a Famista-style view from behind the plate and pitching a Moero!! Pro Yakyuu-style centre-field view. A pennant mode lets players grow, with batters' builds changing and pitchers learning magic pitches. Idol and comedian teams play alongside the twelve regular clubs. Series quirks include hit-by-pitch brawls, a drunk invading the field and zoomed fine plays. The next version, Heisei Gannen Ban (1989), added player editing.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Baseball is universal; names are Japanese but not needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Horizontal-scrolling shooter: pilot the Vic Viper against the Bacterian forces of Gofer, collecting capsules to power up through the Gradius selection bar, across stages heavily rearranged from the arcade.
dossier: Konami's Famicom Gradius II, arriving just nine months after the arcade game, as a largely original arrangement rather than a straight port. It drops the 'GOFER no Yabou' subtitle, and most of the music and stage layouts are new. For example, the first stage adds a Salamander-style prominence area, and stage 2's boss is the Famicom Salamander's original boss Giga. Technical tricks let it show four options and play some DPCM voice samples, and its spread bomb is unusually powerful. The force field is the only shield, rolling options are added, and there are no Option Hunters, while difficulty barely rises on later loops. Two players alternate, with player 2 flying the Lord British. The difficulty was lowered for Famicom players.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Shooter; the English power-up bar is all that needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Triathlon game: choose one of six international athletes and compete in swimming, cycling and running stages, each with its own controls, plus a harder special mode.
dossier: K Amusement's triathlon game, which recreates the swim, bike and run legs. You pick one of six athletes from different countries and race rivals in each stage, and each discipline plays differently. A separate Special Mode makes things stranger and harder: escape a pursuing shark in the swim, cycle through outer space under attack from UFOs, and run through a night-time city where obstacles are hard to see. The cartridge title is spelled 'The Triathron'.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Sports action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Road cycling race around Japan: ride for Team USA, Japan, France or Italy on a 4,000 km coastal tour between major cities, managing energy, bike damage and spare bikes, and keeping your ranking.
dossier: Tokyo Shoseki's road-cycling game, developed by Advance Communication. The goal is to ride all the way around Japan, a 4,000 km race across the countryside between major coastal cities. You choose a rider from Team USA, Japan, France or Italy. You lose if your bike is wrecked with no spare left, if you run out of energy, or if you fall below a set ranking. Passwords save progress through the long tour.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The riding is visual, but status and management text is Japanese, and progress is saved by password.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Motorcycle racing game from Varie that supports a dedicated controller; the sources give no further gameplay detail.
dossier: Varie's racing game, developed by Human. The ja.wikipedia master list notes that it supports a dedicated controller, and FamiWiki classes it as racing for one player. There's no ja.wikipedia article in the research snapshot, so the controller itself, the courses and the play structure aren't documented in the sources consulted. Before buying, check whether a copy includes the dedicated controller and whether the game is playable without it.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — A racing game; presumably playable without reading, though not confirmed.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: Supports a dedicated controller (per the ja.wikipedia master list); the controller's details are undocumented here.

gameplay_summary: Turn-based RPG without levels: lead Firion's rebels against the Palamecian Empire, with characters growing from what they do in battle and weapons and spells improving with use, plus a keyword-memory dialogue system.
dossier: Square's second Final Fantasy, by the same core team (Sakaguchi, Nasir Gebelli, Uematsu, Amano) with Akitoshi Kawazu on design. The Emperor of Palamecia has summoned monsters from hell to conquer the world, and the orphans Firion, Maria, Guy and Leon lose their homeland of Fynn. There are no experience levels or classes. Stats grow from what each character does and suffers in battle, and every weapon type and spell levels up with use, so anyone can become anything. It was novel but full of quirks: tricks that hurt long-term growth, and heavy armour that becomes a handicap. Key words in dialogue are highlighted and can be memorised, then asked about or shown as items to other characters, which steers the story.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A story RPG built on Japanese dialogue; the keyword-memory system means reading is essential.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. A North American NES version was developed to a sample ROM but cancelled.

gameplay_summary: Video pinball on a tall four-screen table themed on the New York skyline, for one to four players in turn.
dossier: HAL Laboratory's console version of its 1984 MSX pinball game. The table is four screens tall, roughly the length of two real pinball tables, with two screens themed on the New York City skyline and a bonus screen at the top showing clouds and a blimp. One to four players take turns. Reviewers of the NES version praised its realistic ball movement and flipper action.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Pinball; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Rollerball (North America 1990).

gameplay_summary: Famista update: arcade-style baseball with fielding errors, adjustable batting orders, a larger pitching staff and random 'hot' players who hit with more power.
dossier: Namco's 1988 Famista, which imports many features from its PC Engine and arcade World Stadium games. Fielders can now bobble or drop the ball, with error rates set per team. You can rearrange the batting order before a game, though not swap in bench players, and the pitching staff grows to four starters and two relievers. New here are 'hot' players: two random starters get extra power, everyone is hot in the 'Lucky 7' seventh inning, and holding Select through a cycle brings up home- or away-favouring modes where a whole side is hot. That idea later became a special mode in the arcade Super World Stadium. Results are reported in a fictional sports paper.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Baseball is universal; player names and the newspaper are Japanese but not needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Family Trainer mat game based on the TV game show Takeshi's Castle; the sources give no gameplay detail for this sequel.
dossier: Bandai's second Family Trainer game based on Takeshi's Castle, Beat Takeshi's TV show in which ordinary contestants storm a castle through absurd physical challenges. Like its predecessor, it's played on the Family Trainer floor mat, which the ja.wikipedia master list confirms is required. There's no game-specific article in the research snapshot, only the TV show's English article, so the stages and how they differ from the first game are unconfirmed.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Physical mat play; menus may be Japanese but nothing essential to read, assuming it follows the first game.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: Requires the Family Trainer mat (Famicom expansion port).

gameplay_summary: Free-scrolling cute shooter: guide the winged ship Opa-Opa through multi-zone rounds, destroy each zone's enemy bases, warp between zones, and spend coins in cloud shops on weapons and engines before the boss.
dossier: Sunsoft's Famicom port, by Sanritsu, of Sega's 1987 Mark III sequel to Fantasy Zone. Ten years after the first game, a new invasion threatens the Fantasy Zone, and Opa-Opa flies out again. At the end he faces the mastermind, a copy of himself, and his father's appearance moves him to tears. You scroll freely left or right, Defender-style. Each round is split into several zones linked by blue warp gates that appear when you destroy bases, and a single red warp leads to the boss once every base is down. A power meter replaces instant death. Cloud shops in fixed places, some hidden until shot, sell parts and upgrades. On Famicom, most music loops are shortened and the colour count is reduced.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Shooter with English shop text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Space fleet strategy based on Yoshiki Tanaka's novels: as Reinhard, plan fleet movements at different speeds, secure invasion routes and bridgehead planets, and push on to the Alliance capital Heinessen.
dossier: Kemco's Famicom game of Yoshiki Tanaka's space opera, subtitled 'Waga Yuku wa Hoshi no Taikai'. You play Reinhard von Lohengramm and aim to take Heinessen, capital of the Free Planets Alliance. It isn't faithful to the source: Oberstein and Hilda command fleets, an original Admiral Hauser appears, and Caselnes and Patrichev lead Alliance fleets. Underneath is a distinctive strategy game of scheduling fleets that move at different speeds, establishing invasion routes and holding bridgehead planets. Admirals differ only in fleet speed, except Yang Wen-li, whose presence counts every Alliance fleet in the same sector as 1.5 times its strength, which makes him very hard to beat with equal forces.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Strategy menus, admiral names and reports are Japanese text.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Bullet-Proof Software's Famicom Tetris: rotate and drop tetrominoes to complete and clear lines as the pieces speed up.
dossier: Bullet-Proof Software's Famicom Tetris, based on its own Japanese computer versions of Alexey Pajitnov's game. It's a separate version from Nintendo's NES Tetris, with its own rules. Notably, BPS's version uses line-quota stage clears, which Nintendo's doesn't. Pieces fall into the well, you move and rotate them, and full rows disappear. The ja.wikipedia master list notes that it was released before the Tetris licensing dispute came to light, and sales continued afterward with Nintendo's approval. Nintendo's own NES Tetris only reached Japan in 2024, through Nintendo Classics.

The ja.wikipedia system description is for the arcade and notes that the Famicom version differs slightly. Its cover-based play influenced Shinobi and Time Crisis.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Rolling Thunder by Tengen (unlicensed, October 1989): the same Arc System Works port under a different publisher.

gameplay_summary: Life-themed board game for up to four players: roll through a lifetime from kindergarten to old age, building a face from parts at the start and playing mini-games such as tests, singing contests, casino games and Arkanoid.
dossier: Taito's first Bakushou!! Jinsei Gekijou, a sugoroku board game that takes you through a whole life in the vein of Takara's Game of Life, but starting in kindergarten. Before playing, each player builds a face from interchangeable parts, fukuwarai style, and making silly faces is half the fun. Board events include school, marriage and the casino, and mini-games include a 100 m race, slots and cards, school tests and entrance exams, children's singing contests and singer auditions, kart racing and driving tests, a flight test, 'Bio Attack' and even Arkanoid. One to four can play, with the computer filling empty seats. Players 3 and 4 share controllers or use a multitap. Box art is by Tong King Show.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Board events and life milestones are all Japanese text; tests and quizzes need reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: Supports a multitap for four players.

gameplay_summary: Cinematic sci-fi command adventure: in 2061, astronaut Hayao Takema investigates the silenced Halley's Comet probe ship and confronts a deadly alien, with story-linked mini-games and music central to the final battle.
dossier: King Records' Famicom port of Enix's 1987 computer adventure, by Chunsoft, with music by Koichi Sugiyama, including the theme 'Aoi Mugen'. In 2061, researchers gather at the space station J.E.S.U.S. to sample Halley's Comet. When the first probe ship, Comet, goes silent, Hayao Takema flies over alone, finds its crew dead, and barely escapes a monstrous alien with the sole survivor, Eline, and worse awaits back on the second ship. It's a command adventure with cinematic touches and story-linked mini-games, and music plays a key role in the final fight. On Famicom, the robot FOJY was redesigned as a comic character, adult-oriented scenes were changed or cut, your later partner is always Eline, and there are no game overs.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A story-driven Japanese text adventure.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Pinball collection starring Namco characters: classic pinball, a bingo-style 'nine ball', head-to-head battle flippers and sports-style tables, across seven tables and four modes, with table-nudging.
dossier: Namco's pinball game, developed by KID (ja.wikipedia credits Artman). It has four modes and seven tables, with six Namco characters each playing differently. The Pac-Man mode is standard high-score pinball. Nine Ball has you bet money and shoot nine balls into bingo-style patterns, and finishing in a target range reveals a secret command. Battle Flipper is a Pong-like duel on tables with flippers at both ends. Sports pinball turns the table into something like a soccer or hockey field. You can nudge the table with B and right on the D-pad. The North American Rock 'n Ball replaced the Namco cast with generic characters, and the Japanese tables are harder, with bumpers spaced differently.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Pinball; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Rock 'n Ball (1990), an altered version.
japanese_version_notes: Features Namco characters (Pac-Man etc.) and a harder table layout; the NES version uses generic characters and larger arches.

gameplay_summary: Chapter-based adventure with action sequences based on Daijiro Morohoshi's manga, in which a boy learns he's the reincarnation of Yamato Takeru.
dossier: Tokyo Shoseki's Famicom version of the 1988 MSX2 game based on Daijiro Morohoshi's Jump manga Ankoku Shinwa. Schoolboy Takeshi learns from a stranger that his father was murdered, finds the cave his father was heading for, and is drawn into destiny as the reincarnation of Yamato Takeru, a story steeped in ancient Japanese myth, Buddhism and SF. ja.wikipedia describes the game as an adventure with action elements, cleared chapter by chapter, with the catchphrase 'Crossing 1,600 years, the dark god revives!'. It's included in the 2018 Classic Mini Famicom Jump edition. The sources don't describe the gameplay in detail.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A story-heavy adventure rooted in Japanese myth; text is essential.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Ninja JaJaMaru RPG: with Princess Sakura, travel Japan solving three yokai incidents in any order, each a chapter with its own levels and gear, then tackle the final chapter.
dossier: Jaleco's third Ninja JaJaMaru-kun game, a four-chapter RPG. The lord asks JaJaMaru to investigate yokai trouble: a crow tengu has stolen the ninja village's secret scroll, Edo's townsfolk have been turned into yokai by an O-nyuudou, and the dragon god of Ryuujin Mountain is abducting people and holding back the rain. Princess Sakura insists on coming along. The first three chapters can be played in any order, with levels and equipment reset for each. Clear all three to unlock the finale, which carries over your last chapter's state. JaJaMaru has attack arts but little power to cast them, while Sakura heals but is fragile. Itako mediums in towns give passwords. It was planned in North America as 'Taro's Quest' but never released.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A Japanese-text RPG; dialogue, menus and kana passwords.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. A North American release as Taro's Quest was planned but not released.

gameplay_summary: Into-the-screen jet combat: fly an F-14 through waves of enemy fighters, shooting and launching missiles, rolling to dodge, and using a timed afterburner boost.
dossier: Sunsoft's Famicom port of After Burner II, despite the box title, and the title screen says 'AFTER BURNER II'. There's no throttle, but pressing Start lights the afterburner for a burst of speed, carrying over II's features. Using a large ROM, it fakes rotation and scaling with stored patterns and plays some voice samples and percussion through DPCM. Some cartridges even carry ROMs stamped SEGA. The carrier you launch from is renamed from the arcade's 'SEGA Enterprise' to 'SUN Enterprise'. After the ending, starting again begins a much harder second loop whose speed climbs sharply stage by stage.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Shooter; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Scrolling military gun shooter: as commando Roy Adams, shoot your way through six stages of enemy territory with a gun cursor or light gun, managing ammo and grenades, to rescue five hostages.
dossier: Taito's home version of its 1987 arcade hit, which defined the machine-gun style of light-gun shooter. As special forces operative Roy Adams, you shoot through six horizontally scrolling stages to rescue five hostages. Each stage has its own objective and effects; for example, after the jungle you interrogate a soldier to learn where the prison camp is. The Famicom version supports the Kōsenjū light gun (and the Zapper on NES), and can also be played with the standard controller.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Shooting; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Operation Wolf (North America 1989).
japanese_version_notes: Supports the Kōsenjū light gun as well as the standard controller.

gameplay_summary: Command-menu adventure in a deadly castle: as the last hero-king, explore Castle Shadowgate keeping a torch lit, solving puzzles with items, to stop the Warlock Lord summoning the Behemoth.
dossier: Kemco's second MacVenture conversion after Déjà Vu, from ICOM's 1987 adventure. The Warlock Lord is trying to summon the demon Behemoth, and you, last of a line of hero-kings, have to get through his castle. Commands like move, examine and open are aimed at things in the picture, and a lit torch beside the command list can itself be used. At least one torch must always be burning, or you stumble in the dark and break your neck, and torches are scarce, so they act as a time limit. The 'self' command lets you use items on yourself, swords and poison included, with predictable results. The castle is full of deaths to discover. FamiWiki notes the Japanese text is infamously poor.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A text adventure in Japanese, and the translation is notoriously awkward even for native readers.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Shadowgate (North America 1989).

gameplay_summary: Baseball with a league season: choose one of twelve NPB-modelled teams, play a 30-game round robin against your league with battery-saved stats, then win the Japan Series.
dossier: Data East's baseball game. You pick one of twelve NPB-inspired teams (all names are parodies) and play a 30-game round robin against your league's other five clubs, which was rare then. Win the pennant and you face the other league's champion in the Japan Series. Stats like batting average and home runs update live and save to battery. An open-game mode pits you against powerful OB and foreign all-star teams. It's full of visual touches: bullpen and pinch-hitter preparation, hero interviews or hanging heads after games, managers whose expressions change at time-outs, and distinct player faces. The title screen says 1988 because it was originally due in December 1988. There's also a bug where runners take on a foreign batter's skin colour.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Baseball is universal; names and stats are Japanese but not needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Stock-trading life sim sequel: now Matsumoto's apprentice with a wife and child, turn ¥4 million into ¥7 billion in two years and reach 'Expert' level 70, balancing the market against family life.
dossier: Imagineer's sequel to Toru Matsumoto's stock sim, again with art by Keisuke Yamashina, partly reusing characters from his manga Kattobi Heart. Having become Matsumoto's apprentice, you now have to grow ¥4 million into ¥7 billion within two years and reach level 70, Expert class. You start married with a six-year-old child (oddly old-faced), all named by you. The private-life side goes strange: neglect your family for stocks and your HP falls and your wife gets angry or leaves until you buy her a ring, and it includes mistresses and drug use that no console game would include today. A system planner tracks stocks, deposits, property and favourites. It saves daily to battery, and resetting without quitting halves your money.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Trading menus, financial terms and family dialogue are all Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling platformer: as Garfield, kick past mice, spiders and birds through timed areas over a week, searching for Odie, who has been snatched by a gang of alley cats.
dossier: Towa Chiki's Garfield game, developed by Mars Corp and based on Jim Davis's comic strip. One Monday Garfield notices Odie is missing, apparently taken by the 'Iron Claw' gang of alley cats, and sets out to find him. It's a side-scrolling action game. You walk, crawl while crouching, jump, and attack with a low judo-style kick, and you have to reach each area's exit door before time runs out. Mice, spiders, birds and other animals get in the way, and there are a few limited-use power-ups. It wasn't popular, and the few who played it consider it kusoge. It never came out in North America, despite Garfield's fame there; reasons suggested include licensing and the game's quality.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Platforming with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Vertical-scrolling dragon shooter: as Prince Lace transformed into a dragon, breathe fire at air targets and bomb ground enemies across nine stages, collecting power-ups along the way.
dossier: Namco's Famicom take on its 1987 arcade shooter, developed by Now Production. It's both an arranged port and a story sequel: Lace, son of the original hero King Amul, has to stop the sorcerer Galda from reviving the demon Zawel. It keeps the arcade's nine stages but trims music and enemies, and its graphics fall well short of other versions. In exchange it adds its own touches: an opening, conversation scenes with the shrine maidens Sheila, Lyla, Silky, Tora, Yunico and Eris, life refills between stages and extra lives. There's an easy Gold Dragon mode for beginners, with more life, full auto-fire and fewer stages, alongside the normal Blue Dragon game. A hidden Select-button trick in the Blue Dragon credits is notorious.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Shooter with English text; the story scenes are flavour.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Dragon Spirit: The New Legend (1990).

gameplay_summary: 'Psychic training' adventure supervised by spoon-bender Masuaki Kiyota: pass clairvoyance, psychokinesis and precognition tests at a psychic school and around Psychic City to finally meet Kiyota.
dossier: Namco's notorious 'develop your ESP through the Famicom' adventure, supervised by the TV psychic Masuaki 'Esper' Kiyota and originally titled 'Psychic People'. In the first half you go through basic training and a graduation exam at a psychic school under Kiyota's direction. In the second you take on events in Psychic City to hone your powers, and meeting Kiyota at the end clears the game. Every task is one of three mini-games. Clairvoyance means guessing a face-down card or a hidden object, precognition means guessing which lamp lights or which car comes next, and both are five-way guesses. Psychokinesis tasks like bending spoons or blooming flowers have you 'concentrate' while pressing A ten or twenty times. In practice it's almost pure luck, and critics mocked it accordingly.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Instructions, Kiyota's guidance and events are Japanese text, though the guessing itself is luck.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Grand strategy across 12th–15th century Eurasia: as Temujin or a rival ruler, manage economy and armies, father heirs and appoint loyal family generals, and conquer the known world.
dossier: Koei's Famicom port of its 1987 PC strategy game Aoki Ookami to Shiroki Mejika: Genghis Khan, produced by Kou Shibusawa with music by Yoko Kanno. It set the series' template. The ordo system has you take wives and father children, and blood-relative generals matter because they never betray you, whereas others may rebel or defect, and there's no loyalty stat to stop them. There are two campaigns. Mongol Conquest (1175) is single-player as Temujin uniting Mongolia. World Conquest (1206) supports up to four players, choosing among rulers across Eurasia from England to Japan. You keep the economy stable, draft and train armies, and attack neighbours. It was also the first Koei game to have you search for talent.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Strategy menus, reports and events are all Japanese text.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Genghis Khan (1990).

gameplay_summary: Open-world brawler with RPG elements: as Kunio, with rival-turned-ally Riki in co-op, fight gangs across town, collect dropped money and spend it in shops on items that raise your stats.
dossier: Technos Japan's third Kunio-kun game and the first of its 'Downtown' line. Set a few months after Nekketsu Kouha Kunio-kun, it has Kunio team up with his old rival Riki to take on Reihou Academy, which is behind a wave of trouble. The fighting is the series' brawling, with weapons like brass knuckles, steel pipes and trash cans to swing or throw, but now in a non-linear open world. Beaten thugs drop money, which buys items in shops that raise your stats, giving it RPG elements. Two players can play together. The North American River City Ransom changed graphics, names and setting, recasting Kunio and Riki as Alex and Ryan.

nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as River City Ransom (1990).
japanese_version_notes: The original Kunio-kun version: Kunio and Riki against Reihou Academy, with Japanese school-delinquent styling; the NES version renamed characters and changed graphics and setting.

gameplay_summary: Action-adventure based on Go Nagai's Devilman; the sources give no gameplay detail.
dossier: Namco's Famicom game based on Go Nagai's Devilman, in which Akira Fudo merges with the demon Amon to fight demons hidden in human society, developed by Isco. gameplay_summary: Overhead dungeon action prequel to Dragon Buster: as the hero Carl, pick buildings on a round map, explore dark dungeons with a bow and limited arrows, take each dungeon's key, and fight the dragon on Dragon Mountain.
dossier: Namco's Famicom-only sequel to its 1985 arcade Dragon Buster, set before the first game. The hero Carl is out to recover the sword of good and evil from the Dragon King. As before, you choose dungeons on a round map, find the exit and finish at Dragon Mountain, but the action is rebuilt as an overhead shooter. Dungeons start dark and light up as you explore. Carl fights with a bow whose limited arrows bounce off walls, and they can hit you too, and there's no magic. His clothes change colour from blue to green, yellow and red as he takes damage. Stay too long and the unkillable centipede Wilder appears. Room guardians drop keys, fire arrows, shields and fairies, and collecting four fairies gives an extra life.

nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Brutally hard dark-fantasy platformer: as the wizard-prince Randy, shoot fireballs through six stages of demons and learn a new spell from each boss to cross obstacles such as lava.
dossier: Irem's Famicom action game, steeped in heavy-metal references. In the 666th year of the world of magic, the Crimson Kingdom falls to the Black Slayer, Demon King of the Underground Dark Empire. Emperor Ronnie IV sends his infant sons Randy and Zakk to another dimension with his servant Ozzy, and seventeen years later they return as wizard kings to fight. Across six stages you defeat a boss at the end of each, and some bosses teach spells such as one that freezes lava. It draws comparisons with Getsu Fuuma Den and Castlevania, and is widely considered one of the hardest games on the system. Retro-Bit gave it its first worldwide NES cartridge release in 2018.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. Retro-Bit's 2018 worldwide NES cartridge is a modern reissue outside the original-era NES set.

gameplay_summary: Horse-race prediction software for Japan's JRA central racing, the first on the Famicom; the sources give no further detail.
dossier: Nichibutsu's horse-racing software, which the ja.wikipedia master list identifies as the Famicom's first JRA (central horse racing) prediction program, meaning a betting aid rather than a racing game. gameplay_summary: First-person Sherlock Holmes adventure: travel France, Austria and Germany solving a mystery set by Professor Moriarty, meeting ten other characters, with kana passwords.
dossier: Towa Chiki's third Famicom Holmes adventure, developed by Another. It follows Hakushaku Reijou Yuukai Jiken and Kiri no London Satsujin Jiken, in which you guided Holmes and Watson around London collecting clues and shillings for cab fares. This time the first-person investigation goes abroad, through France, Austria and Germany, with Professor Moriarty issuing the 'challenge from M'. Ten other characters can be met. You can start new or continue with a password in Japanese characters. Like the rest of the series, it was released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Action platformer: switch between the four turtles, to rescue April, defuse dam bombs, save Splinter and destroy the Technodrome to beat Shredder.
dossier: Konami's first TMNT game, released in Japan as Gekikame Ninja Den before the cartoon or film had reached Japan. It went on to sell about four million copies worldwide. In this version's story, the ninja Hamato Yoshi was turned into a rat when his disciple Oroku Saki betrayed him, and the 'MT gun' also mutated his four pet turtles. Now Splinter's only daughter April has been kidnapped by the Foot Clan. You start as Leonardo and can switch at any time to Raphael, Michelangelo or Donatello. gameplay_summary: Baseball with team building and battery-saved seasons: create a team, set up a league and play a season, with simple timing-based batting and pitching and unusually realistic, forgiving fielding.
dossier: SNK's baseball game, often called the best on the system, and the first baseball game with battery backup. That let you create and customise teams, set up a league, play a season and keep cumulative stats. Pitching is simple (curves, fastballs, change-ups, sinkers) and batting is a level swing that comes down to timing. Fielding was the big step forward: realistic but helpful, with off-screen fielders drifting toward fly balls, catches on anything nearby, and diving and jumping plays. It became the start of a long SNK series.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Baseball is universal; team editing uses simple menus.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Baseball Stars (1989).

gameplay_summary: Three Kingdoms RPG: lead Liu Bei's army of up to seven generals from the Yellow Turban rebellion onward, fighting armies of soldiers, using tactics in place of magic, and recruiting captured enemy generals.
dossier: Capcom's RPG based on Hiroshi Motomiya's manga Tenchi o Kurau, separate from its arcade game of the same name. Starting from the Oath of the Peach Garden and the Yellow Turbans, Liu Bei's forces put down rebels toward unifying China. It follows history roughly up to Liu Zhang, but skips any showdown with Cao Cao and episodes like Red Cliffs. It adds a few original generals but not the manga's heaven and demon worlds. Your formation holds up to seven generals, the front five fight, and the one appointed strategist sits at the back. Soldiers act as HP, and 'tactics' replace magic, powered by the strategist's intelligence. Most random battles are against named enemy generals, who can be captured and recruited.

nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Destiny of an Emperor (1990).

gameplay_summary: Kung fu action RPG: as Jack and Ryu, explore an overhead world map of Chinaland, fight ordinary enemies in action battles and bosses in command-menu battles, and level up to drive out the demon clan.
dossier: Culture Brain's second Super Chinese, and its first as Nintendo's own licensee (the original came out through Namco). It adds RPG elements to the first game's stage-clear kung fu action, and its system set the series' template. You travel an overhead field map. Grunts are fought in fixed-screen action fights like the first game, while big bosses switch to command-select battles. The brothers are renamed Jack and Ryu, and the story becomes a slapstick adventure aimed at younger players, as they take on the demon clan that has seized Chinaland. A bonus 'sports day' mode lets two players, or one against the computer, play its mini-games. Famitsu scored it 21/40.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The action is visual, but town dialogue, shops and boss command menus are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Little Ninja Brothers (1991).

gameplay_summary: Digital version of gunjin shogi (the military hidden-piece board game), arranged in a modern style; the sources give no further detail.
dossier: SOFEL's take on gunjin shogi, the traditional Japanese hidden-identity military board game, where pieces' ranks are concealed and an umpire decides each clash. There's no game article in the research snapshot and FamiWiki has no description, so its rules variants, modes and the meaning of its comic subtitle aren't documented in the sources consulted.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Board-game play is visual once the pieces are learned, but piece names and menus are Japanese.

gameplay_summary: Idol-manager parody RPG: as the manager of the struggling idol trio Child's, tour Japan's department stores and halls winning over 'enemies' with flattery instead of fighting, gaining popularity and new songs and skits, to reach a concert at Tokio Hall.
dossier: Namco's black-humoured parody RPG starring Child's, a real comedy idol group produced by comedian LaSalle Ishii's agency. Ishii's name is on the box but he was barely involved. Child's debuted and flopped, and agency boss Kozo Ishii tells you, the 'chosen manager', to make them stars. You tour Japan on promotional gigs, and when you meet 'enemies' you flatter them ('yoisho') until they become fans. Experience is replaced by popularity, and levelling adds songs and comedy routines to their repertoire. The goal is a successful concert at the star venue 'Tokio Hall'. nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: SD Gundam war sim: move capsule-style mobile suit units across 30 maps, capture factories to build more units, and resolve fights in real-time action battles.
dossier: Bandai's second Gachapon Senshi game, the sequel to the Disk System's Scramble Wars, and one of the earliest console war sims. It fixes its predecessor's weaknesses: up to twelve units can move per turn, and the computer thinks much faster. Units can now be built at captured factories as well as at your base, up to seven production sites, and a factory captured mid-production keeps building for its new owner. nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Single-screen action puzzle: flip the floor tiles of a 5×7 grid to knock enemies into the walls, collecting the items revealed underneath, alone or with a co-op partner, to rescue the hero's girlfriend.
dossier: Game Freak's debut, and the first independently made game sold commercially on the Famicom. Satoshi Tajiri's team built their own development tools, reverse-engineered the hardware using Family Basic, and brought Namco a nearly finished cartridge. Tajiri's idea was that a new action game needs a new verb, here 'flip'. Each stage is a 5×7 floor of panels, and flipping them knocks enemies into the walls and uncovers items, which leaves room for tactics, collecting, discovery, co-op and competition. Enemy behaviour isn't random. In Japan the hero Carton and his partner Parton have to rescue his girlfriend Jenny, kidnapped by his jealous younger sister Quinty and their three brothers. The game's success encouraged Tajiri toward Pokémon.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Puzzle action with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Mendel Palace (1990).
japanese_version_notes: The Japanese framing has Carton rescuing Jenny from his little sister Quinty (the title character); the NES version renames them Bon-Bon and Candy and changes the backstory.

An imprisoned soldier breaks out of his cell and fights through four stages, the POW camp, a warehouse, the jungle and the enemy base, against foot soldiers, choppers, armoured trucks and motorcycles, before facing the enemy general and escaping by helicopter. language_barrier_reason: LOW — Brawling action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as P.O.W.: Prisoners of War (1989).

gameplay_summary: Detective adventure: as police detective J.B. Harold, investigate the murder of a wealthy womaniser in the small American town of Liberty, travelling a grid map of locations to interview suspects and gather clues.
dossier: SETA's Famicom port of Riverhillsoft's 1986 computer mystery Murder Club, the first J.B. Harold case. In the sleepy town of Liberty, wealthy womaniser Bill Robbins is found murdered, and the list of suspects keeps growing. As detective J.B. Harold you visit locations on a grid map, interview people and search for clues to work out who did it and why. The series is known for realistic, photo-like illustrations and scenarios that dig into the relationships behind each crime. The original sold 200,000 copies. The sources describe the series and computer original rather than this Famicom port's specifics.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A text-heavy mystery; interviews and deductions are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling beat 'em up: as a street fighter, punch and kick through ninja-filled streets, trucks and sewers to rescue the kidnapped President from the Dragon Ninja.
dossier: Namco's Famicom release of Data East's 1988 arcade brawler Bad Dudes Vs. DragonNinja. 'Rampant ninja related crimes' culminate in President Ronnie, a thinly veiled Ronald Reagan, being kidnapped from the White House, and a pair of street brawlers set out to get him back. The arcade's attitude-filled premise and intro made it famous. It was one of America's top five arcade earners of 1988. The available sources cover the arcade version; there's no game-specific Famicom article in the research snapshot, so the home port's own differences aren't detailed.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Brawling action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Bad Dudes (1989).

gameplay_summary: Film-tie-in RPG with an unusual system: as the girl Maria, search beyond the pyramids for her missing parents, fighting with summoned spirits alongside her and growing without experience points.
dossier: Kemco's RPG made with the 1988 Japanese-American film White Lion Densetsu: Pyramid no Kanata ni, as part of a Dentsu-commissioned project planned by Data Brain. Tetsuya Kurahashi handled almost all of the scenario, maps, characters and battle design, under the concept of 'pack in as many new ideas as possible'. A legendary white lion once terrorised Egyptian villages before fleeing into a cave called the Gate of Hell. Years later, Maria's parents went to investigate and never returned, and now grown, she sets off to find them. Maria fights directly but can also summon spirits with items to battle beside her, and there's no experience system: battles give money, and she grows another way. The game also lets you avoid killing.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A Japanese-text RPG with an unconventional system that needs reading to understand.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Ghost Lion (1992).

gameplay_summary: Go study software: replay famous games automatically or move by move, and take a rating test that grades you from beginner (to 2-kyu) through intermediate (4-kyu to 2-dan) to advanced.
dossier: Hect's first Igo Shinan, the start of a series that ran to Igo Shinan '94, Hect's last Famicom release. It's a study tool rather than a match program. You can watch classic games ('meikyoku') replayed automatically or step through them by hand, and take a strength test placing you as beginner (up to 2-kyu), intermediate (4-kyu to 2-dan) or advanced. This first edition holds 21 classical, 21 modern and 21 handicap games. Later entries swapped in games by historic masters such as Dosaku and Shusaku. Famitsu gave it 21/40.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Go itself is language-independent, but the menus and rating test are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Zelda-style overhead action RPG loosely based on the film: as Willow Ufgood, explore a world with sword, shield, spells and items, gaining experience in real-time combat and talking to villagers for help.
dossier: Capcom's console Willow, a separate game from its side-scrolling arcade Willow of the same year, and loosely based on the 1988 Lucasfilm movie. It's an overhead adventure in the vein of The Legend of Zelda. Willow Ufgood, mostly travelling alone and only briefly meeting other characters, fights with swords, shields, spells and items, and levels up from real-time combat. Villagers give advice and items, there's no money (everything is found), and progress is saved with a password rather than a battery. At the start, Elora has already been taken by Queen Bavmorda, and the elder sends Willow on his way.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The action is visual, but villagers' advice and the password are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Willow (North America 1989).
